experiment.question: With Collectd at 200 threads and 50 to 100 ms of per-PDU latency, where does the collection cycle stop completing, and does the pool still bind before the processor?
experiment.plan: Hold the latency injection from the 100-thread search (netem delay 75ms 25ms on the simulator's SNMP interface) and the 200-thread pool the sweep chose, grow the fleet from 4,000 in steps of 500 to 5,000 and then 250, one 900 s window per rung, and stop at the first rung that fails. The fleet was then left at the failing rung overnight for 7.75 h with nothing else running, which turned a one-window verdict into a measured deficit. Search upward only: nl6 has no selective delete.

jvm.flags: JAVA_HEAP_SIZE=10240, JAVA_INITIAL_HEAP_SIZE=8192, -XX:+UseG1GC, -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=4 (systemd drop-in), Prometheus JMX exporter on 9299.

workload.generator_scenario: nl6 v0.28.0, cisco_crs_x.json, 144 interfaces per device, SNMP v2c, 10.42.0.0/16 one /24 per 250 devices; uniform 50-100 ms per-packet delay injected on the simulator bridge to stand in for a real agent's response time

figures.title: Collectd thread pool occupancy across the four fleet sizes
figures.note: JMX gauge from Collectd itself. Each rung is a 900 s window separated by a provisioning step. The pool ceiling is 200 now; it is reached in bursts from 4,000 and held in every sample at 5,250.

figures.title: Collectd pending queue, rolling one-minute peak and floor
figures.note: The floor is the pass test. A floor that returns to zero every cycle is a fleet that completes; a floor that stays up is backlog. At 5,250 it never touches zero.

figures.title: Collectd task completion ratio and collectable services
figures.note: The ratio is a sawtooth that resets at every cycle boundary and its median depends on where the window sits in the cycle, which is why it is no longer part of the pass criterion. Services are divided by 1,000 to share the axis, so 5.0 is 5,004.

figures.title: Collections completed per second against the rate each fleet requires
Samples per second delivered against the rate the fleet requires
figures.note: The completion counter multiplied by the 1,738 samples every fleet collection carries, decoded from the topic. Required is the collectable service count over the 300 s interval, times the same 1,738. A window integral is the honest rate; the rolling rate is shown for shape.

figures.title: Core CPU against the thread pool: the control
figures.note: Node Exporter for CPU, JMX for the pool, on one axis. Threads block on the SNMP round trip, so the pool fills while the processor stays idle. This is what thread-bound looks like.

figures.title: Core JVM heap and old-generation collections
figures.note: Shown so the reader can see it was checked: no old-generation collection occurred in any rung, and the heap cycled between 3 and 9.5 GiB under a 10 GiB ceiling.

figures.title: Minion CPU and the SNMP bridge under injected latency
figures.note: The Minion executes the walks that the Core's threads wait on. Under latency it, too, is waiting rather than working.

series.label: SNMP on the sim bridge, Mbit/s

figures.title: The queue floor over 7.75 hours held at 5,250 devices
figures.note: The fleet was left at the failing rung with nothing else running. The rolling 5-minute floor is the backlog that survives every cycle; it climbs at a steady 80 tasks an hour, which is the pool's measured shortfall.

answers.question: With 200 threads, where does Collectd stop completing its cycle at 50 to 100 ms per PDU?
What does the failure at 5,250 look like over hours rather than one window?
How many metrics does this fleet produce, and at which rung?
What runs out at 200 threads, and what does not?
What did doubling the pool buy against the 100-thread search?
How was each rung measured, and what changed in the pass criterion?

gaps.question: Was the 4,000 rung measured the same way as the others?
gaps.why: It ran under the earlier criterion, failed on the completion-ratio median (0.9854), and was re-judged a pass on the counter integral (99.2%) after the criterion was replaced. Its window is otherwise identical. The three later rungs ran under the final criterion from the start.

gaps.question: Is uniform latency the right shape?
gaps.why: netem's default is uniform between the bounds. Real agent response time is heavy-tailed. Under Little's law the same mean should give the same pool occupancy, but that was not tested here.

gaps.question: Does the overnight hold generalise?
gaps.why: It is one fleet at one size with no provisioning, no traps and no rescans in flight. It measures the pool's shortfall cleanly and nothing else; a production Core would have other work competing for the same threads.

gaps.question: Do the simulated agents behave like real ones under latency?
gaps.why: netem delays every packet equally. A real agent that must query line cards delays the first PDU of a table walk more than the rest. The per-PDU cost is right; its distribution across a walk is not.

gaps.question: Is 250 the right resolution for the knee?
gaps.why: The last pass and the first fail are 250 devices apart. The overnight deficit locates capacity at 5,247 services per cycle, but that is one window's arithmetic on the failing side, not a measured pass at 5,200.

gaps.question: When does a growing backlog become missed collections?
gaps.why: Over 7.75 h the floor rose 615 tasks while every task that ran completed. At some depth the scheduler starts skipping cycles rather than delaying them; that depth, and the hours it takes to reach, were not measured.
